payingUser: The owner-operator of a small local business with no designer and no design budget - a cafe, food truck, market stall, deli, salon, barber, nail studio, gym, personal trainer, tutor, florist or repair shop - who needs a menu, a price card, a table tent or a window sign with the prices they actually charge, on the phone they already hold.
paidUnit: A pack of credits, where one brand set costs 2 credits (one generated background at $0.050 plus one absorbed recognition at $0.010) and becomes five print and display artefacts because the typesetting happens free on the device. Starter $14.99 buys 5 sets, Studio $34.99 buys 15, Workshop $79.99 buys 40; a one-time $19.99 unlock removes the print-export limit and the brand-kit limit and costs nothing to serve.
momentOfPayment: At the first server-cost operation after the free starter grant of 10 credits (5 sets, $0.30 per device to serve) is spent - the moment the owner wants a background generated for the list they have just laid out - with the set's price shown before the tap; and again at the first export past the free limit, where the one-time unlock is offered beside the packs and never in front of the first card.
distinctnessSentence: One typed price list becomes five print and display artefacts - menu, price card, table tent, window sign and story post - from one generated background, with every price typeset on the phone from the shop's own data instead of drawn by a model, and exported as a print page with no watermark.
day1RevenuePath: A shop that installs installs to print today's card, not to browse: it imports the CSV or photographs the old card, spends the 5 free sets, and hits the first paid background inside the first session - so day 1 collects a pack price from a user whose need arrived with them, and the measured warm-up is that the app is opened when a price changes or the season does.

rejectedArchetypes.revenueReason: One price against a recurring per-use cost: a shop printing 40 sets a month costs 40 * $0.060 = $2.40 every month while a $19.99 unlock nets $16.16 once, and a 400-set month for a small chain costs $24.00 - the unlock turns negative in its first month and stays there.

A rewarded-centric app earns about $0.05 per DAU per day, so 1000 DAU is $1500/month, while the free tier this job needs - one set per user per day - costs 1000 * $0.060 = $1800/month: the free tier costs $300/month more than the ads earn before any other cost, and at the cheaper background-only set ($0.050) it breaks exactly even at zero margin.
A Play Console price with no discovery lever (docs/monetization-strategy.md#4), and it cannot fund a per-use provider cost any better than the single unlock can.
Banned by the owner (2026-10-01), absent from ARCHETYPES and machine-refused by parseEconomics with no exemption path; not weighed.

assumptionsUnverified: No conversion rate is measured anywhere for this shelf: the only figure the factory holds (about 1-3% for a one-time in-app purchase) is labelled UNVERIFIED in docs/monetization-strategy.md#4, so the sales-per-month column is a division of the target, not a forecast.

The pack ladder ($14.99 / $34.99 / $79.99 / $19.99) is this role's proposal, not a market price: every enriched competitor card on the price-card shelf printed free with in-app purchases, so no competitor's Android price anchors it.

The effective Play fee tier for this account is unverified; at 25-30% the net factor falls to 0.7130970-0.6655572 and K rises to 3.5058-3.7562, which raises the per-set floor to $0.21035-$0.22537. The Studio pack's $2.3327 per set still clears it, but the ladder has less room.

The provider costs are the factory's own registry values, not a live fal read taken today: the decider is re-reading each endpoint's model page, which docs/research/2026-10-16-generation-capability-inventory.md lists under what is still missing.
Whether small-business owners will install a phone app for print work at all is the kill criterion and is unmeasured until this slot's own store/outcomes.json reading exists.

The generation registry, adapter, routes and server are slot-local rather than a published capability, and the background operation (O-07) is enabled in the registry but has never been reachable from a shipped UI, so its end-to-end readiness is unverified until it is driven once.

Whether an image model actually mangles prices was not tested in this session (no generation was run, because the server's provider key is not set for a recon run): the decider is one authenticated call to the flux endpoint with a prompt containing 7.90 and 12.50, and the design holds either way because the measured complaint is lost price data rather than model spelling.

Whether a print shop accepts the exported PDF as a print-ready imposition (page size, bleed, colour space) is unverified: no print shop was consulted, and the promise is a print page rather than a printer's imposition.

Every demand reading here came from one signed-out Play session on one storefront with a display cap of roughly 30 cards, and relevance order is not size order, so a larger incumbent can sit below the cut.
The name Placard was not trademark-searched and no Play title search was run: the decider is a Play search for the exact title plus a class-9 search of TMview, USPTO, EUIPO and WIPO.
notes: Capability pairing: purchase_led_repeat_sales requires the billing capability to be enabled, and ads must stay disabled - an ad-led version of this app loses money by construction (see rejectedArchetypes).

The one structural fact that makes this plan cheap: one generated background feeds five deliverables, because the layout and typesetting work happens on the device for free. That is why the price-to-cost ratio is 38.9x rather than the 3.3x a credit-priced recipe runs at.

A server is required and its cost is stated rather than discovered: the generated background is a provider call with a server-only key, so the factory's existing generation server (server-authoritative credits, Play-confirmed purchases, two-phase reserve/settle/release, $25/day spend cap, release-on-failure) is the shape, and its cost is the $0.060 per set above.
